Giving up?

This is a mix between TTC and vent post, tbh.

We’re almost at the 6 month mark since my blighted ovum at 8 weeks, and I’m starting to lose hope for ever having a baby. We got pregnant 3 months into TTC, and now that it’s been nearly 6 months since my MC, I’m beginning to feel resigned to the fact that we’ll just never have children, and it breaks my heart.

Our next step is to try a medicated cycle with IUI, but everything I read says that’s a low chance of success, and all I hear about IVF is how expensive it is, and that’s not guaranteed, either.

I never imagined a life without children, but now that I’m here I feel like I have to, and the thought of that makes me feel so purposeless and empty.

I just needed a place to vent. Thanks for reading.

Menstrual cycle changes post vaccine

My last period appeared a week earlier than usual, I had tender swollen breasts and menstrual cramps - I've never suffered menstrual cramps. I also noticed a lot more 'clots', so much so I wondered for a moment if it wasn't an early miscarriage.

Now I'm getting the tender breasts and cramps again, and again it's a week earlier than usual.

My cycles are normally very regular. I have a hormonal IUD which I've had two years, it caused some irregular bleeding the first few months but didn't stop my periods or change my cycle length.

The vaccine is the only factor I can think of which may be the explanation. It's not a big deal, I just like to know why my body isn't doing it's normal thing...and hoping cramping is temporary!

Has anyone else experienced changes like this, is it just coincidence?

MMC d&e vent

Just here to vent, and see if anyone had a similar experience.

Just this week I learned at 14 weeks, my baby didn’t have a heartbeat.

Husband (36m) said something that broke my (39f) heart. How do I process it?

This is whether long… but bear with me, please.

Husband (36m) and I (39f) have been together for 12 years, 8 married and have a 2yo. In the beginning, we talked about been a child free couple, and that was fine with me. When Covid hit, I took a look at my life and saw that we both have stable jobs, didn’t have any grand plans (to buy a house, to chance professions) and thought that a kid wouldn’t really interfere with what ever life plans we had or would have. We talked at length about trying to conceive, and how a kid would give us a different experience out of our lives that seemed already so settled.

In the next 6 months, I got pregnant 3 times. The first was an anembryonic pregnancy - the egg gets fertilized and implants into the uterus but doesn't develop into an embryo. The next month, I got pregnant, but had a miscarriage at 10 weeks. It was easily the worst days of my life. Then, the very next month, I got pregnant again, and 39 weeks later, we had our baby boy.

The first 3 months were a whirlwind of sleep deprivation, chaotic days with me crying, the baby not nursing properly - he was admitted with jeunesse for lack of feeding-, had a tong tie, and torticollis. It was one of the most challenging periods of our life. We spent a lot on medical bills!

We didn’t have any support from family nor friends. We have a cleaning lady that comes in once a week. Our baby boy was one of those that would fuss +1h to get down to nap just to rest for 30-40 min, and would only sleep while nursed. I was fully on baby duty and exhausted. Husband was the one doing groceries and most of the meals, doing dishes, laundry.

 I went back to work at 7 months. We decided to hire a nanny. My husband rose to the part and took care of the baby by himself on weekends and holidays – I am essential worker (work on the subway) and have a work schedule of 3 x 2 (work 3 days in and off for 2), sometimes the 3 days in are Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

I know this is hard on him because his all by himself with our son until the nanny arrives or for most of the weekend – I work a 10 hour shift – from 5am util 3pm. To ease things for him, when I arrive, I take the shorter shower you’ve ever seen, don’t wash my hair on weekends, and take the baby duty util bedtime, when he comes in and reads a book.

Fast forward 2 years, and things have improved a ton! A 2yo is such a different kid! He’s so smart, asks for whatever snacks he wants, has his favorite books, is learning how to ride a balance bike, and even states when is tired and needs a rest – takes 2h-2h30 long naps, yay!  

I feel that motherhood chanced me a lot… for the better! I’m in awe of how he’s developing, how much his vocabulary is improving by the day, how smart and fun/ funny he is! He has the sweetest voice, gives the warmest of hugs, has the best laughter! I’m so in love, so infatuated by this tiny human that I made!

I am scheduled for an abortion tomorrow

I have an appointment for a medical abortion tomorrow and I am distraught. I (34F) have a 4 year old and a 2 year old, and we are finally getting out of that intense caregiver phase that comes with infants. My sleep is finally starting to get back on track, I’ve gotten my post partum body to a place I’m happy with, and my career is skyrocketing with opportunities in a job I get a lot of meaning out of. I found out I’m four weeks pregnant and I have been beside myself with what to do.

My immediate response was remorse and dread at the thought of pressing the reset button on my life, on once again losing my bodily autonomy, on once again pausing my career and sacrificing any personal development. I really feel like I will lose my sense of self if I go through with this. I love being a mother and it is a part of my identity, but it is not my sole identity, and to step back from the individual I’ve slowly been building back up over the last few years is honestly devastating. 

Even with all of that, I do not feel like my reasons to terminate are good enough. My husband and I can financially support this child, we have a stable healthy relationship, it is early but presumably it is a healthy child…

I feel like a selfish piece of shit and have been beside myself on this. It feels wrong to decide whether my life is more important than someone else’s, and it doesn’t feel like my reasons are valid. They’re selfish, and I don’t know how I can come to terms with accepting that. I also would never want to bring a child into the world who I may resent, I hope that wouldn’t be the case but I don’t know how I would feel. The guilt is eating me alive, I am so torn on how to feel. My husband is supportive of whatever I choose, but ultimately it is my choice. I feel so lost, and that whichever choice I make will be wrong.

1. COUNT KICKS.  If you're 28 weeks or over, you can start counting kicks.  This is the MOST important thing you can do.  In places where providers have started pushing kick counts stillbirth numbers have dropped substantially. Knowing your baby's patterns, when they're most active, etc. Is so important.

2. The idea that babies slow down and move less when they get bigger or sleep more is a myth.  If you notice these changes, talk to your provider.  If your provider dismisses your concerns keep pushing!  

3. Dread/your intuition screaming at you that something isn't right is actually a very good reason to get checked out.  Sometimes its just anxiety, but it can be a REALLY good indicator that things aren't okay.


I hope that this information helps.  Its not meant to scare anyone, just inform.  Stillbirth is so much more common that anyone talks about, and often we never even find out why it happened (we still don't know what happened with Amélie).

The Answer to The Question, "When Was Your Last Period?"

"Fuck the fascists. I'm not telling." 

I take birth control continuously, and do not have a period. When healthcare providers ask "When was your last period," they will not accept the answer "I don't know/I don't have periods." They insist on putting down a date and will make one up if I don't give them one (I know they are just checking boxes and are required to do this). This has admittedly been a minor annoyance, but with the [judge in Texas repealing privacy protections for women's reproductive health information](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/biden-reproductive-privacy-rule-halted-by-federal-judge-in-texas?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email), I think it's time that we put our foot down and refuse to self-report this information. 

Hey, I get that providers have to protect themselves from liability and may need to do a pregnancy test or have you sign a release. But, in light of these exculpatory tools that protect them, they absolutely do not need to endanger us by requiring the date of our last period, unless amenorrhea is a concern during diagnostics, or it is actually relevant to the reason for the visit.

Let's say the date of your last period can be used in a criminal trial to estimate if: you could have been pregnant; how far along you could have been; or whether you engaged in activities which could have harmed a fetus between the time of pregnancy loss and the date of your last period--according to the health records they can subpoena. If that is the case--which it is looking more and more like it might be--then healthcare providers are literally aiding the prosecution of their patients by routinely requesting and recording that information, knowing that they can't block a court from accessing it (and many times handing it over voluntarily when not required by law, because they are afraid--as reported by Jessica Valenti in her Jun. 19, 2025 newsletter).

I am not going to be rude to healthcare workers just doing their job, but the answer to that question should no longer be expected from us. It is endangering us.

Things I never realized before I had one

1. You might know immediately what you want to do, but it doesn’t make it any easier to navigate the emotions. For me, it was a tragic certainty… but I was still certain.  

2. The stigma of abortion prevents people (even in places where it is legal) from getting the information they need. All my questions felt shameful and the search for answers often leads to pro-life rhetoric. People outside of this situation have the privilege of seeing this as only a morality conversation…when it is also a healthcare and safety conversation.

3. I myself and many others go it alone or with only one other person supporting us. Especially those who found themselves pregnant after a traumatic situation, because it may feel too soon to open the wound far enough to share your story just yet. It’s such a lonely thing and we are so strong. 

4. It’s not always quick or easy to access. Depending on the person, their body and the level of access and support they have, it can mean weeks of waiting as their body changes in ways they do not want—all while having to work, take care of any existing children, and putting on a smile for the world outside. Each day can feel like being held hostage in a body that is not your own. 

5. Everyone has a deeply personal story. Our reasons vary but we all have come to this very difficult choice for a reason and it’s so damaging to be invalidated by people who think they can look at you for 5 minutes and make this choice seem so black and white.

6. Sometimes in making the decision, you go into fight mode. You do whatever you can in your power to get through it and you realize how strong you can be when you need to. Sometimes it’s not until later that you really process.

7. You are now a part of a centuries long legacy of women— some of whom didn’t get to choose when they wanted to… some of whom had to go to extremely unsafe measures to be able to choose. Going through this I’ve been thinking of them, and am grateful that their time informs our present. 

8. Most importantly, we will all be okay. We will make it through this choice, and navigate it emotionally. It may take a lot of time, and this will change your perspective the same way it has changed mine. But it doesn’t change you. You are still a sister, a friend, a good person. You are still everything you were before and more. You have gone through something difficult but this doesn’t define you and it never will. 

These are truths I never considered until I went through it myself. I’m not sure the point in this, but it was therapeutic for me and I hope someone finds it relatable and comforting to know someone else feels similarly and we will get through It.
